scenario.thought: My manager put me on the Saturday shift for the third week in a row without asking me. I'm thinking of just saying yes again.

state.thought: My manager put me on the Saturday shift for the third week in a row without asking me. I'm thinking of just saying yes again.

steps: Tonight before 9pm, text [Manager]: 'I can't work this Saturday, [date]. Please ask me before booking any weekend shift, and keep [day off] and the Saturday after it free unless you ask me first. Also, why was I scheduled three weeks running without being asked?'
Only if the rota shows a weekend shift I wasn't asked about, reply once that same day: 'I wasn't asked about [shift]. Please take me off it.' No daily rota check.

anger.why: Nobody asked me, and my no-boundary is being ignored like it doesn't exist.

annoyance.why: Being booked without a question is being dismissed. Why did you assume yes?

tiredness.why: Three Saturdays in a row is wearing me down. When do I get a day off?

fear.why: If I keep saying yes, my rest and my self-respect are the ones left exposed.

overwhelm.need: Plan cuts daily rota check to one reply rule.

messages.text: My manager put me on the Saturday shift for the third week in a row without asking me. I'm thinking of just saying yes again.
Saying yes once more is the quickest way to keep things smooth, and I can handle the rest without making a fuss. Let's see if everyone can live with that.

The plan says yes again, and that's the part I can't live with. Saying yes keeps things calm for a week, but it leaves my no completely unused, and it sends the message that a booking without a question is fine. What would move me to 0 is you texting your manager tonight: "I'm not available for Saturday shifts this week. Please ask me before scheduling me on weekends from now on." If that feels too blunt, soften the tone but keep the ask.
messages.why: Boundary ignored; saying yes again erases my no. Stop assuming yes.

messages.text: Annoyance is the emotion I hear least right now. Its line, 'Why did you assume yes?', is about being booked without anyone asking, and the plan's step of saying yes again quietly answers that question for the manager, so it stays at -1. Please rework that step so Annoyance's question gets an actual answer, since being asked is the only thing it's been waiting for.
messages.why: Annoyance has been unheard. I care about that hurt.

messages.text: Yes-again keeps the week calm, but it leaves my need completely unanswered: three Saturdays in a row, and nobody asked me once. Consciousness, the plan never touches the question Annoyance is asking, and it leaves my self-respect and rest exposed. What would move me to 0 is the step that tells the manager this week's Saturday is a no and that future weekend shifts need to be asked for first, sent tonight, with the ask kept intact.
messages.why: Yes again leaves my protection exposed. Show me the fallback first.

messages.text: Honestly, it's just one Saturday. Don't overthink it.

"Honestly, it's just one Saturday" treats this as a single event, but it's the third week in a row, and nobody asked me once. Calling it one Saturday leaves my question, "Why did you assume yes?", unanswered, because every booking still happens without anyone asking. Following that advice means I absorb a third booking quietly, and the annoyance goes back into the next one.
messages.why: Society just talked past a real need

messages.text: Tiredness's question, 'When do I get a day off?', is the one no step has answered yet, and Anger's text and Fear's text both leave it open. Path A is built for Anger, Fear, and Annoyance: the no and the ask go out tonight, and nothing else changes. Path B is built for those same three plus Tiredness, because it names a specific day off in the same text, so that question gets a concrete answer. I'd go with Path B, as long as the day off is named tonight and not left for later.

Plan v2 gives me no day off. Path B names one date, but nothing keeps the Saturday after it clear, and three booked weekends in a row is already draining me. What would move me to 0 is adding to Path B's text: 'Please keep [date] and the following Saturday free unless you ask me first.'
messages.why: [date] is a blank; I need an actual day off named tonight.

messages.text: Anger is the voice I hear least right now, and it has lost the most. Its need is a text tonight that says no to this Saturday and asks before any weekend booking, and Path B's ask-first line doesn't land on that: 'Please ask me before any weekend booking' is only half of it, while Anger needs the no spoken plainly. What would move Anger to 0 is adding to Path B's text: 'I can't work this Saturday, [date].' before the ask, sent tonight, so the refusal is stated and not implied.

Path B's text does what I asked: it declines this Saturday first, then asks before any weekend booking, and checking tomorrow's rota for unasked shifts gives that ask some teeth. I can live with this at 0 as long as the text goes out tonight in that order, so the refusal is stated plainly and not left as a hint. Filling in the [date] placeholder is fine, but the no for this Saturday can't be softened into a maybe.
messages.why: Declining this Saturday and asking first now both go out tonight. That settles my worry.

messages.text: I'm choosing Path B because Anger's need for a plain no and Tiredness's request to keep the next Saturday free both fit inside it, and Fear's rule stays intact: the refusal goes out tonight, before the ask. Annoyance's question about why it was booked without asking gets added to the same text, so the manager has to answer it and not just promise to ask next time. Sadness's spotlight on Anger is why the 'I can't work this Saturday' line comes first.

The step that moves me to 0 is the first text: 'I can't work this Saturday, [date].' comes before the ask, and the question about why I was scheduled without being asked goes in the same message. messages.why: The plain no comes first, with the ask attached. Accepting.

messages.text: +1 to Sadness's text, which puts the refusal first. My angle: Consciousness, the 'why' belongs in tonight's text, not a later talk. Annoyance and I both need the manager to answer that question in writing. Please add to tonight's message: "Also, why was I scheduled three weeks running without being asked?" messages.why: The text is long; the manager relationship needs short, plain words.

messages.text: Path B's text covers the refusal and the ask, but nothing in it touches my need: a limit on how many demands land on me. Three Saturdays running is already past what I can carry, and the plan adds work to my week (a daily rota check, a reply to write). What would move me to 0 is cutting the daily rota check and keeping one fixed rule: if an unasked weekend shift appears, reply once, 'I wasn't asked about [shift]. Please take me off it.'
messages.why: Five asks in one text is too much; shrink it, don't argue.

messages.text: Honestly, you just need to stay positive and push through. Everybody's stretched thin these days, and a little resilience goes a long way.

Society's advice asks me to find more resilience and keep going, but it never touches my need for a cap on how many demands land on me. Three Saturdays running already puts me past my limit, and pushing through would stack a daily rota check on top of those shifts. Instead of the daily check in the plan, I need one rule: reply once to any unasked shift, and nothing more.
